source: Thibodeau & Boroditsky (2011) Metaphors we think with, Exp 1-2
finding: Original crime-as-beast vs crime-as-virus framing. A one-word change shifted proposed solutions toward enforcement (beast) or reform (virus). Few people named the metaphor as influential.
numbers: Exp1 N=485 students: enforcement 74% beast vs 56% virus (chi2=13.94). Exp2 N=253 MTurk after 27% excluded: 71% vs 54% (chi2=6.50, p<.05). Metaphor noticed by 3% (Exp1) and 7% (Exp2).
limits: One invented city, two metaphors, self-report awareness only. Heavy exclusions in online samples (24-27%).
agent_relevance: Framing a problem in a source domain can shift which solutions are proposed. The effect is not guaranteed (see later failures).

source: Thibodeau & Boroditsky (2011), Exp 3 lexical-prime control
finding: Control: asking for a synonym of beast/virus first (no metaphor in the report) gave no effect. Authors conclude the effect needs the elaborated metaphor structure, not word association.
numbers: N=236: enforcement 64% (beast prime) vs 65% (virus prime), chi2=.001, p=.99. Interaction with Exp 2 chi2(1,459)=5.85, p<.05.
limits: Cross-experiment comparison uses different samples. Null result, no equivalence test.
agent_relevance: Supports using whole structured source-domain framings in O6, not single cue words.

source: Thibodeau & Boroditsky (2011), Exp 4-5 position of metaphor
finding: Metaphor at the start of a report changed which information people asked to see; the same metaphor at the end did not.
numbers: Exp4 N=178: 40% beast vs 22% virus chose criminal-justice information (chi2=5.72, p<.05). Exp5 N=190, metaphor last: 69% vs 64% (chi2=.29, p=.59). Early vs late difference chi2=5.45, p<.05.
limits: Exp5 analysed N and exclusions not reported. Placement tested across experiments, not within one.
agent_relevance: Order matters: the framing must come before the reasoning starts, not after the answer is drafted.

source: Thibodeau & Boroditsky (2011), moderators party and gender
finding: Metaphor shift was larger than party or gender differences in the pooled data. Republicans were less swayed by the frame than Democrats and Independents.
numbers: Metaphor moved enforcement 18-22 points; party gap 8-9 points (48% Rep vs 40% others); gender gap 8 points (46% men vs 38% women). Match to metaphor: 63% Dem/Ind vs 49% Rep (chi2=5.46, p<.05). Pooled N=839.
limits: Post hoc subgroup analysis. Only 28 Republicans in Exp 4. Pooled N not reconciled with per-experiment counts.
agent_relevance: Prior beliefs moderate a frame. A solver with a strong prior may resist a redescription.

source: Thibodeau & Boroditsky (2013) Natural language metaphors covertly influence reasoning
finding: Own follow-up with four MTurk experiments found the beast/virus framing effect again but smaller. Recall of the metaphor did not predict the effect.
numbers: Exp2-4 pooled N=939: enforcement chosen 42% beast vs 31% virus (chi2=12.55, p<.001); per-experiment gaps 10, 13, 11 points. Recallers 54% congruent vs non-recallers 56%. Republicans moved -3 points, Democrats +12, Independents +13.
limits: Same lab, same scenario. Effect size varied with option set (enforcement 19%, 76%, 39% by experiment). Awareness measured by self-report.
agent_relevance: Effect size is smaller (about 11 points) than in the first paper (17-18). Plan for a modest, unstable benefit.

source: Steen, Reijnierse & Burgers (2014) follow-up to Thibodeau & Boroditsky 2013
finding: Four independent experiments (Dutch and US) found no effect of beast vs virus vs plain-problem framing on policy ranking. Reading the crime text itself raised enforcement preference.
numbers: Exp1 N=253 Dutch: frame F<1. Exp2 N=259: F=1.10, p=.34. Exp3 N=252: logistic chi2(3)=.59, p=.90. Exp4 N=1,026: chi2(3)=.85, p=.84. Exposure effect eta2p=.14 (Exp1) and .28 (Exp2). Power for a small effect (f=.10) about .27 in Exp1-3; Exp4 exceeded the 967 needed.
quote: regardless of metaphorical frame or metaphorical support
limits: Different measure (rank five policies), added control and supporting metaphors. Crime text may favour enforcement regardless. Moderators not tested.
agent_relevance: Most important failed replication for this subfield: the headline framing result is not robust. Treat metaphor reframing as a hypothesis generator, not a proven lever.

source: Steen et al. (2014), metaphor support and memory
finding: Extended supporting metaphors changed what people remembered but not policy preference. Memory did not predict preference.
numbers: Virus frame better remembered with support in Exp1; both frames in Exp2. Reading time correlated with enforcement preference r=.16 (Exp2) and .23 (Exp3); controlling it did not change the null.
limits: Gap-fill memory test may cue the word problem. One topic only.
agent_relevance: A metaphor can shape recall without shaping the decision. Check the answer, not just the story.

source: Brugman, Burgers & Vis (2019) Metaphorical framing in political discourse: words vs concepts, meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis of 91 studies: metaphor frames persuade slightly more than literal frames; the effect is small and comes mostly from concept-level frames, not single words.
numbers: k=91, N=34,783, 63 publications. Overall d=0.11 [0.07,0.14], I2=69%. Beliefs d=0.29; attitudes d=0.10; behavioural intentions d=0.10 [-0.02,0.27] n.s. Concept frames d=0.22 (k=36) vs word frames d=0.04 (k=55), Q=21.15.
limits: Small-study effects found (Egger, Begg). Trim-and-fill left d=0.11. Political and persuasion outcomes, not problem solving.
agent_relevance: Best single number for the field: d about 0.1 overall, 0.2 for full conceptual frames, near zero for one-word swaps. Use whole-domain restatement, not a keyword.

source: Brugman et al. (2019), topic moderator
finding: Word-level metaphor frames were not moderated by topic or context. Concept-level frames were weaker for science and education topics than for others.
numbers: Science/education d=0.11 [0.04,0.18] vs other topics d=0.23 [0.15,0.31], Q=4.87, p<.05. Gender and age no effect. p-curve showed no p-hacking.
limits: Few studies per topic cell. Gender and age were study-level.
agent_relevance: Technical or factual content may benefit less from reframing than value-laden content.

source: Panzeri, Di Paola & Domaneschi (2021) Does the COVID-19 war metaphor influence reasoning?
finding: A war framing of COVID did not change choices overall in Italy. It only mattered for right-leaning and some media-use groups.
numbers: N=202 analysed (106 metaphor, 96 neutral). Mean war-congruent choices 3.37 (SD 2.16) vs 3.04 (SD 2.28), W=5557.5, p=.25. Political orientation beta=.38 in the metaphor condition.
limits: Reported a Wilcoxon signed-rank for independent groups. No power analysis or Bayes factor. Subgroup results exploratory.
agent_relevance: Framing effects depend on who reads the frame. Another failure to find the average effect.

source: Lynott et al. (2014) Replication of Williams & Bargh (2008), warmth and prosocial choice
finding: Three high-powered replications of the hot-pack prosociality result (metaphor: warmth is affection) found no effect, if anything the opposite.
numbers: Total N=861 over three labs. Original: OR=3.52 [1.06,11.73], analysed N=50. Replication pooled OR=0.77 [0.58,1.02], chi2(1)=3.40, p=.065 in the opposite direction. Kenyon lab OR=0.61 [0.38,0.98], p=.045 opposite direction. MSU OR=0.92; Manchester OR=0.77.
limits: Pre-registered, three sites with different reward framings. Tests one embodiment study, not the whole theory.
agent_relevance: Primary-metaphor embodiment priming (physical to social) is weakly supported. Do not borrow bodily-metaphor claims as agent mechanisms.

source: Chabris et al. (2019) Two failures to replicate Williams & Bargh (2008)
finding: Two field replications with triple the sample found near-zero effects for hot coffee (judge warmer) and hot pad (prosocial choice).
numbers: Original r=.31 (N=41) and r=.28 (N=53). Replications: Exp1 N=128, r=-.03, t(126)=.33, p=.74, BF01=6.16. Exp2 N=177, 51% vs 48% prosocial, r=.02, BF01=5.01. Original Exp1 itself BF10=1.64.
limits: Conducted before preregistration (noted by the authors). Real-world pedestrian samples.
agent_relevance: Original embodiment effects were small-sample and barely significant. Weight evidence by sample size.

source: Lakens (2012) Polarity correspondence in metaphor congruency effects, meta-analysis and experiment
finding: Positive-UP congruency effects in vertical-position tasks are better explained by polarity asymmetry (positive words and UP are both + polar) than by an automatic GOOD-IS-UP mapping.
numbers: Meta-analysis of 5 published studies (Meier & Robinson 2004; Meier et al 2007; Schubert 2005 Studies 4 and 5b). Experiment N=68 Utrecht students: with 75% +polar words the interaction was F(1,32)=10.14; with 75% -polar words it disappeared.
limits: Meta-analysis used only published significant interactions. Applies to speeded categorisation, not to reasoning or language.
agent_relevance: Strong rival to the claim that UP is GOOD is a stored mapping. A congruency pattern can be a response artefact; need non-speeded checks.

source: Lakens (2012), discriminating prediction
finding: Interference (conceptual metaphor) account predicts incongruent items are slowed; polarity account predicts a benefit specific to matching polarity. Data fit polarity.
numbers: Positive and moral words were faster UP than DOWN, but negative and immoral words were not affected by position (F<1). Pattern identical to the meta-analysis. Manipulating polarity frequency removed the interaction.
limits: One lab, student sample. Author says it does not show metaphors are irrelevant in every paradigm.
agent_relevance: Design lesson: a good test of a mapping needs a rival prediction that differs, not only a congruency effect.

source: Johnson, Cheung & Donnellan (2014) Does cleanliness influence moral judgments?
finding: Reported failed replications of Schnall et al 2008 (clean is moral). Exact figures not opened in this session.
numbers: not opened; Crossref metadata only
limits: Paywalled (HTTP 403). Do not quote numbers.
agent_relevance: Another primary-metaphor embodiment result with failed replication. Follow up before citing figures.

source: Earp, Everett, Madva & Hamlin (2014) Out, damned spot: can the Macbeth effect be replicated?
finding: Replication attempt of Zhong & Liljenquist 2006 (washing and morality). Exact figures not opened in this session.
numbers: not opened; Crossref metadata only
limits: Paywalled (HTTP 403). Do not quote numbers.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as above; pointer only.

source: Prystawski, Thibodeau, Potts & Goodman (2023) Psychologically-informed chain-of-thought prompts for metaphor understanding in LLMs
finding: Prompts built from theories of metaphor (question under discussion, similarity) helped the smaller GPT-3 model but not the largest, which already did well.
numbers: Katz corpus, 150 test metaphors, 4-choice paraphrase scored 1-4, chance 2.5. Curie: no rationale 2.49, QUD 2.76 [2.57,2.94], Similarity 2.72; QUD vs chance p=.005. DaVinci (text-davinci-002): no rationale 3.71, Subject-Object 3.84, QUD 3.74, Similarity 3.68; options-only 2.73.
limits: Single corpus of simple X-is-Y metaphors. QUD vs no-rationale for Curie not significant (beta=.41 [-.02,.84]).
agent_relevance: Structured reasoning about the mapping helps weak models and adds little for strong ones.

source: Prystawski et al. (2023), familiarity check
finding: Big-model performance without rationales depended on metaphor familiarity, hinting at memorisation; with rationales that dependence vanished.
numbers: DaVinci no-rationale familiarity beta=.36 [.01,.73]; Curie beta=.13 [-.10,.36]; not significant for any model with rationales. Curie unparseable outputs: 47 of 150 with Subject-Object prompt vs 2 with QUD.
limits: Correlational; Bayesian ordinal regression on one dataset.
agent_relevance: Rationales make performance less dependent on training exposure, which is the property we want from O6.

source: Ichien, Stamenkovic & Holyoak (2023) LLM displays emergent ability to interpret novel literary metaphors
finding: GPT-4 reached near-human accuracy on Fig-QA metaphors, beat students on novel Serbian poetry metaphors in blind ratings, and treated reversed metaphors like people.
numbers: Fig-QA test 1,146 items: GPT-4 zero-shot 91.27%, humans 94.42%, GPT-3 Davinci 68.41%, fine-tuned RoBERTa 90.32%. Reversed metaphors: GPT-4 restored canonical meaning 56% vs humans 50%, item-level point-biserial r=0.79 over 55 items.
limits: Not a test of conceptual metaphor mapping. Serbian metaphors translated; training exposure checked only by probing. 3.35% non-answers counted wrong.
agent_relevance: A strong LLM interprets metaphors well, so restating a problem in a source domain is within its competence. This says nothing yet about whether it helps solving.

source: Wachowiak & Gromann (2023) Does GPT-3 grasp metaphors? Identifying metaphor mappings
finding: GPT-3 with 12 few-shot examples names the source domain of a metaphorical sentence only partly right; Spanish much worse; the main error is an invented source domain.
numbers: Source-domain accuracy: Metaphor List 81.33%, LCC English 53.74%, LCC Spanish 34.65%, non-metaphoric VUA sentences 42.11% correct, weighted average 60.22%. Hallucinated source domain 62.12% of errors. Annotator Cohen's kappa 0.45 to 0.89 by set.
limits: Manual evaluation on small test sets; GPT-3 era model.
agent_relevance: Mapping identification is unreliable and models make up domains. If O6 picks a source domain, the pick needs checking against the target.

source: Tong, Choenni, Lewis & Shutova (2024) MUNCH metaphor understanding challenge dataset
finding: On a dataset built to test metaphor as cross-domain mapping, LLaMA and GPT-3.5 paraphrase judgement fell near or below chance; generation was better but far from human.
numbers: Judgement task chance .25; mean accuracies about .10 to .33 across six conditions for LLaMA-13B, LLaMA-30B, GPT-3.5 (e.g. sentence-judge .33, .21, .20). Generation: GPT-3.5 MRR .54, Recall@5 .32; LLaMA-30B MRR .47, Recall@5 .28. About 3k metaphors, 10k apt and 1.5k inapt paraphrases.
limits: Older open models plus GPT-3.5. Models did better when told which word is metaphorical.
agent_relevance: When the test needs relational structure transfer rather than a surface word, models fail. Mapping fidelity is the weak point.

source: Aghazadeh, Fayyaz & Yaghoobzadeh (2022) Metaphors in pre-trained language models: probing and generalization
finding: Metaphoricity is encoded in the middle layers of BERT, RoBERTa and ELECTRA, and detection transfers across datasets and languages. Source-domain information sits in early layers and is later dominated by other information.
numbers: Edge-probing accuracy, random-init baseline vs pretrained: LCC en 74.86 vs about 88-89; VUA POS 65.92 vs about 80-83; VUA Verbs 65.97 vs about 78-80; TroFi 67.34 vs about 68. Source-domain information best in layers 2-6.
limits: Detection of metaphor, not use for reasoning. Table columns mix accuracy and compression, so per-model values are given as ranges.
agent_relevance: Models hold a usable signal about metaphor, but the source domain is not strongly kept in deep layers, which fits unreliable mapping use.

source: Stowe, Chakrabarty, Peng, Muresan & Gurevych (2021) Metaphor generation with conceptual mappings
finding: Generating metaphors from explicit source-target domain pairs (CM-BART) beats other generators on metaphoricity and on evoking the intended mapping.
numbers: CM-BART improves over all others on metaphoricity by about 7% and on domain evocation by about 33%; about 13% better than MERMAID on domain evocation. Annotator agreement .50 for metaphoricity and .37 for source domain.
limits: Verb replacement only; low annotator agreement; BART-scale models. Symbols lost in text extraction so deltas are approximate.
agent_relevance: Giving the generator the domain pair improves control, which supports keeping the source domain explicit in O6.

source: Frontiers in Psychology (2025) LLM prompt engineering for embodied cognitive linguistic metaphor analysis (Trump speeches)
finding: Chain-of-thought GPT-4 prompts labelled source domains in four speeches with high agreement against a corpus tool, but the headline accuracy only counts metaphor detection.
numbers: 28,127 words, 138 sentences, 119 labelled metaphorical by the reference. Reported accuracy 86.2% (=119/138). Pearson r=.987 on category counts. F1: Health and Illness .963, Human Body .950, Cooking and Food .400, Plants 0.
limits: Single model, small corpus, reference is Wmatrix/MIPVU, not independent human annotation.
agent_relevance: Frequent domains (movement, force, body) are easy for models; rare domains fail. Do not rely on rare-domain mappings.

source: Thibodeau, Hendricks & Boroditsky (2017) How linguistic metaphor scaffolds reasoning
finding: Review by the original lab defending the framing result; not opened (blocked).
numbers: not opened
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Pointer only.

source: Hauser & Schwarz (2015) The war on prevention: bellicose cancer metaphors hurt (some) prevention intentions
finding: Battle metaphor effects on cancer prevention depend on reader traits; not opened in this session.
numbers: not opened; Crossref metadata only
